title: My marriage is falling apart
seoTitle: When Your Marriage Is Falling Apart: Faith and Real Help
description: For a marriage gone cold, loud, or broken by betrayal: what Scripture says, what to do this week, and where to get help, with safety first.
summary: For the marriage that's gone cold, loud, or broken, and for anyone afraid at home: safety first, then real help.
askedAs: Bible verses for a struggling marriage
What does the Bible say about divorce
I don't love my husband anymore
answer: You may be lying awake beside someone who feels like a stranger, or replaying tonight's fight, or holding a phone full of messages you were never meant to see. Maybe the word divorce has been said out loud, or maybe it only lives in your head. Either way, the promise you built your life around is coming apart, and you don't know whether it can be saved or whether you still want it to be. You don't have to decide that tonight. But if you're afraid of your spouse, or someone at home is hitting, threatening, controlling, or isolating you, hear this before anything else: that isn't a marriage problem you can fix by trying harder. Call or text the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed just below, and get safe first.
happening:
A marriage rarely comes apart in one night, even when one night is when you find out. More often the cracks spread for years, and then everything seems to give at once. You can feel lonelier beside your spouse than you ever felt single, because the one who is supposed to know you best has become the one you can't reach. You may be furious one hour and numb the next, and ashamed that the marriage everyone assumes is fine is anything but.

The usual explanations each hold part of the truth. A counselor may say you're stuck in a pattern, the same argument in a hundred costumes, and patterns can be unlearned. A doctor may ask about depression, drinking, pain, or exhaustion, because illness can drain the warmth out of a person, and what feels like contempt is sometimes a sickness nobody has named. The church will tell you to pray, forgive, and stop keeping score, which is true as far as it goes. What all of them can miss is that *marriage trouble* isn't one thing, and the right first step for one kind can be the wrong step for another.

For some couples the trouble is distance: nobody has done anything unforgivable, but you've become roommates who run a household, and the quiet has gotten comfortable. That's serious, and it can be turned around if both of you will turn. Other marriages are loud, the same fight every time about money or chores or the kids, with both of you keeping score, which is exhausting and more fixable than it feels. Betrayal breaks some marriages open, an affair of the body or the heart or years of lies about money, and if you're the one betrayed, you aren't overreacting; the ground really did move. An addiction to alcohol, drugs, or gambling can crowd a marriage until the sober spouse is managing an illness they didn't choose, and it has to be treated, not only prayed about. Pornography is its own kind of secret, and when it comes to light it lands as betrayal because it is one.

And some marriages are more than troubled; they're dangerous. Abuse isn't only hitting. It can be threats, control of the money or the phone or the car, cutting you off from family and friends, pressure or force around sex, or Scripture and words like submission used to keep you quiet. If that's your home, the problem isn't that you haven't loved well enough, and couples counseling isn't the first step. Safety is. Everything else on this page assumes you're safe. If you're not, the Hotline comes first, and no one, including me, should counsel you to stay in danger to keep a marriage together.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't treat marriage like a greeting card, and it doesn't pretend marriages never break. It opens with a couple naked and unashamed and, one chapter later, hiding and blaming. Each passage is read where it stands: who wrote it, to whom, and why. None of them tells you to stay in danger.

passages.text: The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.” ... For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
passages.reading: Marriage enters the story as God's answer to the first thing he called not good, a man alone, and the chapter closes on two people fully seen and not ashamed. The Hebrew word translated helper is the one the Old Testament uses most often for God himself, as in “He is our help and our shield” (Psalm 33:20), so it names strength brought to someone's side, never a lesser worth. Then comes Genesis 3, where sin sends them into hiding and teaches them to blame. The man who sang “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23) is soon saying “The woman whom You gave me” (Genesis 3:12). If your marriage has gone from song to blame, you're living inside the oldest story there is, and the loneliness you feel beside your spouse is the very ache marriage was made to answer.

passages.text: For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide. But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God. ... My companion attacks his friends; he violates his covenant. His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed.
passages.reading: The psalm's heading gives it to David, and it's about a friend, not a spouse, but anyone betrayed by the person who shares their bed will know every line. The wound is deeper because it came from someone he worshiped beside. Nothing in the psalm tells him to calm down or to examine his own part first. Earlier he wishes for wings like a dove, to fly away and find shelter (Psalm 55:6-8), and Scripture keeps that wish in its prayer book without a word of rebuke. The psalm lets him tell God that his companion “violates his covenant” (Psalm 55:20), and it names the soft voice with war behind it, which is what two-faced cruelty feels like at home. The psalm ends with the trouble unsolved and a choice made: “But I will trust in You” (Psalm 55:23).

passages.text: “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold. ... Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
passages.reading: Paul is writing to a church about people who belong to one another, and no neighbor is nearer than the one across your kitchen table. He doesn't forbid anger; he forbids letting it settle in, because anger left to sit becomes a foothold for something worse. Then he names what long fights are made of, bitterness and rage and slander, and answers with kindness and forgiveness measured by how God forgave you. That forgiveness cancels a debt. It doesn't pretend the debt wasn't real, and it never requires you to stay within reach of harm.

passages.text: Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
passages.reading: You probably heard this at a wedding. Paul wrote it to one of the most quarrelsome churches in the New Testament, a congregation in Corinth split into factions, suing one another, and shaming the poor at the Lord's table. Read as a mirror, it's hard on everyone. But don't skip the middle: love “takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). So “bears all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7) can't mean enduring abuse in silence, because that would make love a partner to evil. The love Paul describes is patient, and it is honest.

passages.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Go show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and offer raisin cakes to idols.” So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. Then I said to her, “You must live with me for many days; you must not be promiscuous or belong to another, and I will do the same for you.”
passages.reading: Hosea's marriage was a prophecy acted out, one prophet told to love an unfaithful wife as a picture of how God loves an unfaithful people. It isn't a rule that every betrayed spouse must take the betrayer back, and it says nothing to someone in danger except that God is not like the one hurting them. Notice what restoration cost: Hosea paid to bring her home, and he set terms that bound him as much as her, a long season of faithfulness before anything was assumed. Reconciliation after betrayal still looks like that. Most of us read this story as Hosea. The text puts God's people in her place instead, loved while unfaithful and bought back anyway, and that includes every one of us.

whyHard:
When a marriage is failing, the easiest explanation is that you married the wrong person, and the next easiest is that the culture has made marriage disposable. There's truth in both, but marriages were breaking long before either explanation was available. The prophet Malachi told the men of Judah, who were weeping at the altar because God no longer accepted their offerings, that the LORD had been “a witness between you and the wife of your youth” (Malachi 2:14). The question put to Jesus was whether a man could divorce his wife “for any reason” (Matthew 19:3). The trouble is older than our age. It goes back to a garden where the first couple learned to hide and to blame, and every marriage since has inherited the reflex.

What our age adds is a new idea of what marriage is for. In 1985 the sociologist Robert Bellah and his colleagues published Habits of the Heart, drawn from interviews with middle-class Americans, and they named one strand of what they heard expressive individualism, the conviction that each of us has a unique core of feeling that must be expressed if we're to become ourselves. They found many people describing love the same way, as a bond worth keeping for as long as it keeps fulfilling the two people in it. There's real good in insisting that marriage involve love and consent. Older arrangements trapped a great many people in cruelty, often women with nowhere else to go, and the church too often called that faithfulness. But when a marriage exists to make me whole, every hard season becomes a verdict on the whole marriage, and the exit is always in view. No marriage can carry the weight of being someone's salvation.

The church didn't resist that idea as much as we like to think. We dressed it up. We sold marriage as the road to happiness and let the Christian family become a kind of performance, so couples in trouble learned to smile through the lobby and come apart in the car. At our worst we protected the institution instead of the person, sending frightened spouses home with a verse about submission or forgiveness. I'm a pastor, and that indictment includes me. A church that makes trouble unspeakable teaches its people to hide.

Scripture's word for marriage is sturdier than a feeling and more personal than a contract. It calls it a covenant, a promise made before God to seek one person's good for life. That is why a marriage can outlast seasons when the feeling is gone, and why real repentance can carry it even through betrayal. It is also why abuse can't be treated as one more hard season to endure, because a promise to seek someone's good is broken, not tested, by the one who makes the other afraid. Whether that breach ends the marriage is a question faithful churches answer differently, and the questions at the end of this page set out how. That it frees you to get safe is not in question. Every kind of trouble on this page (the drift, the war of words, the affair, the bottle, the screen, the fist) grows best where no one is allowed to see. Whether your way forward turns out to be the way back or the way out, it begins with the truth told to someone who can help. Nothing heals unseen.

thisWeek.intro: One week won't mend a marriage, but it can hold a few small, faithful steps. If you're afraid of your spouse, the first step comes before all the others, and the rest assume you're safe with each other. And unless safety requires it, this isn't the week to file papers, move out, or tell the children it's over.

steps.title: If you're afraid, start with safety
steps.body: Call or text the National Domestic Violence Hotline on this page, even if you aren't sure what's happening counts as abuse. An advocate can help you make a safety plan for you and any children. If your spouse checks your phone or computer, use one they can't reach, like a friend's phone or a library computer. Talk with the advocate before you tell your spouse you're leaving, because leaving is often the most dangerous time. If you're in immediate danger, call 911.

steps.title: Tell one person the truth
steps.body: Trouble grows in the dark, so tell one person what's really happening: a trusted friend, a pastor, or a counselor. Choose someone who wants good for both of you, not someone who'll feed your anger or pass your story along, and if you're afraid at home, choose someone who will believe you and put your safety ahead of keeping the marriage together. If your spouse has told you not to tell anyone, notice that. You don't need permission to ask for help.

steps.title: Stop the fight that keeps repeating
steps.body: When an argument starts circling, stop and say you want to finish it well, then name a time to come back, tomorrow at eight rather than *later*, and keep it. When you come back, one of you speaks while the other listens and says back what they heard before answering. The letter of James says that everyone should be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19), and nothing tests that like a kitchen at eleven at night. Stay on one subject.

steps.title: If you've been hiding a sin, stop
steps.body: If you've been hiding an affair, pornography, gambling, debt, or drinking, bring it into the light before it's found. Don't do it alone, and don't do it just to unload your guilt. Talk first with a pastor or counselor about telling the whole truth at once, ending what you've hidden, and accepting that trust returns on your spouse's timetable, not yours. Proverbs is blunt about it: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). None of this applies to a safety plan: if you're quietly preparing to get safe, keep it private and work it out with the Hotline.

steps.title: Make one call for help
steps.body: Call a licensed counselor this week, and if your spouse won't come, make the appointment for yourself. In a marriage that's troubled but safe, one person growing wiser can change the pattern between you, and you'll need support either way. Abuse is different: it isn't yours to fix by changing yourself, and couples counseling isn't safe with an abusive partner. Ask the Hotline or an individual counselor what is.

moreHelp.body:
A pastor and good friends can carry a lot, but some trouble needs people with training or authority. If there's violence, threats, or control, start with the Hotline, and call 911 in an emergency; police and courts can do what no pastor can, including protective orders, which a local advocate can explain. An addiction needs treatment, and your doctor or SAMHSA's National Helpline can point you toward it. If either of you is sinking into depression or thinking about suicide, see a doctor, and call or text 988 in a crisis. If separation or divorce is on the table, a family lawyer can explain your rights around children, money, and your home; getting information isn't the same as filing.

For the marriage itself, look for a licensed counselor who sees couples: a marriage and family therapist, professional counselor, clinical social worker, or psychologist. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about license and training as well as faith. Get names from your doctor, your insurer's directory, or a pastor who knows the good local counselors, then confirm the license on your state licensing board's website. If there's abuse, don't begin with couples counseling; the Hotline doesn't recommend it with an abusive partner, who holds the power in the room and can punish honesty at home.
signs: You're afraid of your spouse, or they have hit, choked, or threatened you.
Your spouse controls your money, phone, car, or who you're allowed to see.
Either of you has talked about suicide, or about hurting the other or the children.
Drinking, drugs, or gambling are draining your money or your days.
You haven't slept, eaten, or worked normally for more than two weeks.
Someone is pressing you to sign papers or give up time with your children.
The same fight has run for months, and you can't get to the bottom of it.
moreHelp.firstCall: When you call a counselor's office, you can say it simply: *Our marriage is in serious trouble, and I'm looking for someone who works with couples.* Then ask whether they're licensed in your state, what they charge, whether they take your insurance, and whether you can start alone if your spouse won't come. If you're calling the Hotline, you don't have to be sure it's abuse. You can say, *I don't know if this counts, but I'm afraid of my spouse.*
moreHelp.cost: Counseling costs vary widely, and insurance may cover individual sessions but not couples work, so ask the counselor and your insurer before you start. Lower-cost help exists: sliding-scale fees, community mental health centers, university training clinics where supervised graduate students see clients for less, and employee assistance programs, which often include a few free sessions. Your church may have a benevolence fund; ask. The Hotline is free, and local domestic violence programs and legal aid offices can often help with protective orders at little or no cost.

helping.body:
If a friend tells you their marriage is falling apart, listen longer than feels comfortable. Don't rush to fix it, pick a side, or pass the story along, even as a prayer request, and remember you're hearing one side of a two-sided story, unless what you're hearing is fear.

If they're afraid of their spouse, everything changes. Believe them. Don't confront the spouse yourself, which can make home more dangerous, and don't suggest the three of you sit down and talk it out. Help them reach the Hotline, and let them make their own decisions about leaving, even when you'd choose differently. Someone who has been controlled needs choices handed back, not taken again.

Pastors carry a particular weight here. When a spouse tells you they're afraid, don't counsel the couple together, don't tell the other spouse what you heard, and don't ask the frightened one to submit or forgive their way to safety. Refer them to the Hotline and to licensed help, and keep being their pastor. If children are being harmed or are at risk, you may be a mandated reporter; the rules differ by state, so learn yours before you need them. This isn't legal advice.
say: Thank you for telling me. I believe you.
This isn't your fault, and you don't have to decide anything tonight.
Do you feel safe at home right now?
I'm not going anywhere. What would help this week?
Would it help if I sat with you while you make the call?
dontSay: What did you do to set them off?
If you submit more, things will get better.
Think of the kids and go home.
helping.next: Check in again within a few days, and keep checking; people in trouble often go quiet when they most need company. Offer something concrete: childcare during a counseling appointment, a ride, a meal, or help finding a safe place to stay. If you're worried about someone's safety, the Hotline's advocates talk with friends and family too. And if the couple is safe and willing, the most useful words may be the plainest: *I'll help you find a counselor, and I'll keep praying while you go.*

prayer:
Lord, you were there when we made our promises, and you've heard everything since. I don't know tonight whether this marriage is dying or only wounded, and I'm too tired to tell the difference. You know what has been done to me and what I have done. Don't let me hide from either.

If I'm in danger, give me courage to get safe, and silence every voice that says you want me within reach of harm. If I'm the one who broke faith, don't let me excuse it. Where there is still life between us, breathe on it. Where there is only a wound, keep it from turning to poison.

Put wise people around us, and give me the patience to listen. Deal with the one I married, in justice and in mercy, as only you can. Hold everyone in this house who is caught in the middle. You are faithful when we are not. Don't let me go. Amen.

faq.a: Not tonight, and not alone. If you're in danger, get safe first; that comes before this question, and separating to be safe is not a sin. Faithful Christians, and whole church traditions, read Jesus and Paul differently here. Some take Jesus at his starkest, “what God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matthew 19:6), and hold that separation may be necessary but remarriage isn't open while a spouse lives. Others read the exception Jesus names for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul's word that a deserted believer “is not bound in such cases” (1 Corinthians 7:15), as real grounds for divorce and remarriage, and some extend that reasoning to abuse. Both guard something true: the permanence of the promise, and the protection of the betrayed. This question divides faithful churches without dividing anyone from Christ. Take it to a pastor who knows you and a counselor who can see the whole picture.

faq.q: My spouse wants a divorce and I don't. What can I do?
faq.a: You can't make another person stay, and pleading, threatening, or tracking their every move usually pushes them closer to the door. You can change your side of the pattern: stop what has hurt your spouse, even if it isn't the whole story, and ask plainly for a pause and for counseling before anything is final. See a family lawyer so you understand your rights, especially if you have children, and keep the children out of the middle. If your spouse leaves anyway, their choice is not a verdict on your worth.

faq.q: Can a marriage survive an affair?
faq.a: Some do, and some come out more honest than before. It takes the affair ending completely, the whole truth told once with help rather than leaking out for months, and a long season in which the unfaithful spouse earns trust back without demanding it, usually with a counselor's help. The betrayed spouse doesn't owe anyone a quick recovery. Forgiveness, trust, and reconciliation are different things: forgiveness cancels the debt, trust is rebuilt by evidence over time, and reconciliation takes both people. You can forgive and still not be ready to trust. Whether you're bound to stay is one of the questions faithful Christians answer differently.

faq.q: My husband watches porn. Is that cheating?
faq.a: You're not overreacting to feel betrayed. Jesus said that “anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28), so Scripture treats this as a matter of faithfulness. It isn't your fault or about your body, and wives struggle with it too. The one caught in it needs more than an apology: honesty about the whole history, accountability someone else can see, and often a counselor. You need care of your own as well. Whether it's grounds for divorce is a question Christians answer differently. If anything you found involves someone under eighteen, report it to the police.

faq.q: I don't love my husband anymore. Is it over?
faq.a: What you feel tonight is real, but it isn't a verdict. The feeling of love rises and falls in long marriages, and it can go flat for reasons that have little to do with your spouse: exhaustion, grief, depression, years of unspoken resentment, or a life so crowded you only meet over logistics. Scripture describes love mostly as something you do, and the feeling often follows the doing. Tell a counselor honestly what you feel and don't, and see a doctor if the flatness has spread to the rest of your life. If what you feel isn't *I don't love him* but *I'm afraid of him*, start with the Hotline.

faq.q: Should we stay together for the kids?
faq.a: Children aren't helped by parents who stay and keep wounding each other, or by a hurried exit either. What shapes them most is what they see. A child who watches two people fight and then repair learns what a kept promise looks like; a child who watches a parent live in fear learns something darker. If your home isn't safe, the answer is simple: safety first, for you and for them. If it's safe but hard, the children are one more reason to get help now, while there's still something to rebuild. Don't make them messengers, confidants, or referees. They didn't choose this, and they shouldn't have to carry it.

slots.note: Where James lands on divorce and remarriage, in his own words: which grounds he holds (sexual immorality, desertion, abuse), whether remarriage is open and to whom, and the tradition his view comes from. The answer to 'Should I get a divorce?' states both readings and deliberately does not land.

For 'Should we stay together for the kids?': if James chooses, a few sentences on being raised without a father and what a child carries from a home that breaks or never formed. Only from James; the answer stands without it.

If James wants it, his own pastoral observation of couples who hide trouble at church, to sit beside the paragraph on the church's performance culture. Only from James; no composite or invented couples.

Any counselors, domestic violence programs, or recovery ministries near Fenton that James trusts enough to name, and whether First Baptist Church of Fenton has a protocol when a spouse discloses abuse. Only from James.

Safety comes first: the answer and What's going on name fear, hitting, threats, control, isolation, and spiritual abuse, and send the reader to the Hotline before any counsel about staying; no passage, step, or answer counsels staying in danger, and the three texts most often misused against victims (1 Corinthians 13, Ephesians 4, Hosea 3) each carry their own guard. Divorce and remarriage: both readings stated with their texts and named as second-order, with no landing for James (slot left). No statistics, no quotations but Scripture, no stories, people, or biography beyond the permitted facts. The Bellah attribution and the Hotline guidance (no couples counseling with an abusive partner, safety planning, safer devices, leaving as a dangerous time, help for friends and family) were confirmed through search results, because direct page fetches are blocked here; the source URLs came from those results and were not opened. Every kit link resolves live and unredirected, and each linked page was read for how it handles abuse. No proprietary program is named or imitated. Read as the person at midnight on a phone, the skeptic, the pastor, and a licensed counselor.
